title: I generated each of these characters with a single prompt
author: Chologism
selftext:
I was very excited to see the quality of Pixel Engine's animations and I spent the last couple of days playing with it and eventually ended up integrating it into my workflow.

My goal was to make it as hands-off as possible so beginners and vibe gamedevs are able to use it as well. 

The stack is pretty simple:

I use my nano banana based asset generation platform for the initial image:  
e.g. "A samurai" , "A brown dog. Isometric" 

And then I just select what type of animations I need and it generates them all in one go. Naturally it's going to mess up sometime so I have the ability to regenerate any from scratch or do some light touch up in manual editor. The example here are all unedited, generated in a single pass.

The next step is to ship a lightweight character controller designed for the target environment (Unity, Godot, Three.js) that way you could instantly move around with the character with 0 coding.

So many possibilities..

Would love to hear what you think about this, and any suggestions are welcome!

replies.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
replies.body:
My game design starts with my ideas but I found that just spitballin’ with normal ChatGPT works pretty good. Chat helps give me the big picture on how to implement and lets me know about possible future pitfalls if I don’t do x or y. Usually for a character or asset or whatever I use normal chat to set things up in Godot, then if it’s something I think will be too complicated I have chat describe what I want to do an create a prompt for cursor. I go back and forth asking chat if what cursor is doing looks like a good idea, revise prompts 2 or 3 times and then let cursor implement. Working pretty good for my simple 2-d platformer! I backup A LOT!

I’m pretty new to this whole thing but that workflow  has been good for me. 

Been making my own pixel art to start and then having Retrodiffusion animate if needed but I’m going to check out what op is talking about.

Hope that helps, hope more experienced people can chime in for us!

# Ninja — black-and-white pixel style

* **Character:** Ninja, black-and-white pixel style

   * Last 3 frames: quickly crouching down to hide
* **Style:** Black-and-white pixel style, simple and bold
* **Layout:** Horizontal row, 1×6
* **Background:** Transparent
* **Use:** Can be used directly in games or animation frame-control systems

* **Action:** Casting a spell + turning around
* **Frames:** 8 frames total, 4 spell-casting frames + 4 turning frames
* **Layout:** 2×4, horizontal arrangement
* **Background:** Transparent
* **Style:** 16-bit
* **Description:** A 16-bit wizard waving a staff to cast a spell, top row 4 frames, and turning around with cloak movement, bottom row 4 frames

# Skeleton Mage

* **Action:** Summoning + dissipating
* **Frames:** 8 frames total, 4 summoning frames + 4 dissipating frames
* **Layout:** 2×4, horizontal arrangement
* **Background:** Transparent
* **Style:** Pixel art, dark color palette
* **Palette note:** Low-saturation dark colors, such as purple-black and gray-white
* **Description:** A dark pixel-art skeleton mage waving a staff to summon souls, top row 4 frames, then turning into smoke and dissipating, bottom row 4 frames. Transparent background, with an eerie atmosphere.
